summary: Raises the susceptibility of the ARPANET to security violations. Its title echoes the opening of a well-known Christmas poem.

eli5.summary: This note points out ways the network could be misused, like checking whether the doors of a house are properly locked.

subtitle: Early ARPANET security vulnerabilities and warnings

tldr.problem: The early ARPANET had multiple security weaknesses: many systems used guessable passwords, TIP access points were publicly listed with no authentication required, and some people enjoyed breaking into systems as a challenge.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC documents three categories of vulnerability and cites recent real incidents, including two major hosts that were crashed and an administrator password compromised by high school students in Los Angeles.
tldr.outcome: This early warning helped motivate better security practices in network systems and demonstrated that network security was a serious problem that required intentional design.

today: RFC 602 stands as an early and remarkably prescient warning about network security. While the ARPANET's authentication mechanisms have evolved dramatically since 1973, the fundamental concerns it raises—weak passwords, unauthorized access, and the human tendency to test security boundaries—remain relevant to modern network security.

sections.title: The Three Main Vulnerabilities
sections.content:
RFC 602 identifies three fundamental security problems in the ARPANET:

Weak passwords: Many users still chose passwords that were easy to guess: their first names, initials, their host name spelled backwards, or sequences of letters that were easy to type in sequence (such as ZXCVBNM). This assumption that physical access controls were sufficient to protect systems made sense locally, but not on a network.

Open access points: The Terminal IMP (TIP) allowed untrained users to access the network with no authentication. TIP phone numbers were posted publicly, like handwritten notes in phone booths and men's rooms. Anyone with a modem could try to dial in.

The challenge: Despite—or perhaps because of—how easy it was to break into systems, some people pursued it as a game. They knew the risks but were drawn to the challenge of defeating someone's security.
sections.eli5: Passwords were too easy to guess. You could dial in without proving who you were. And some people thought breaking in was fun.

sections.title: Recent Attacks
sections.content:
The RFC's authors make clear that this is not a theoretical problem. In recent weeks, at least two major serving hosts had been crashed by attackers who knew what they were doing and took the risk anyway. On a third system, the system administrator's password had been compromised—by two high school students in Los Angeles, no less.

These were not accidental mishaps; they were deliberate attacks on critical systems. The sheer fact that teenagers with modems could compromise major ARPA-supported systems was alarming to the network operators.
sections.eli5: Real attacks had already happened. Actual computers on the network got knocked down. People who shouldn't have been able to get in, did.

sections.title: A Serious Call to Arms
sections.content:
The tone of RFC 602 is unusual for a technical document. Its title echoes the opening of a famous Christmas poem ("The Stockings Were Hung by the Chimney with Care"), framing the warning in holiday language. Yet the message is clear and urgent: network operators should not sit idle in "hope that Saint Nicholas would soon be there."

The RFC's publication signaled to the network community that security vulnerabilities were not just embarrassing bugs to hide—they were a serious concern affecting the reliability and trustworthiness of the entire ARPANET. Systems needed deliberate, careful security design.
sections.eli5: The note uses funny language, but the message is serious: stop waiting for someone else to fix this. You have to lock the doors yourself.
